rows.label: Concept
rows.text: A changing current in one coil induces an emf −M dI/dt in the other. M is the same in both directions and is large when the coils share flux. A steady primary current induces nothing, which is why a transformer needs alternating current.

rows.label: Solved
rows.text: Mutual induction is the emf in one circuit caused by a changing current in a nearby circuit. The changing current changes the flux that links the second coil.  ·  The mutual inductance M is defined so that the flux linkage in the secondary is M times the primary current. The induced emf is −M dI/dt.

rows.label: Key points
rows.text: One coil's changing current induces emf in a second coil.  ·  M is mutual inductance.  ·  It is symmetric.  ·  A transformer uses it.

rows.label: Study notes
rows.text: M is the same either way: a current changing in coil 2 induces in coil 1 with the same M. That symmetry is M_12 = M_21.  ·  M is large when the coils share flux, as on a common iron core, and small when they are far apart or at right angles so that little flux links across.  ·  A transformer is mutual induction used continuously with alternating current. The secondary emf exists only while the primary current is changing.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Mutual inductance needs two circuits.  ·  A steady primary current gives no secondary emf.  ·  M is not always equal to √(L1 L2). That is the maximum, when all flux links.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: The two directions share one M.  ·  Name which current is changing.  ·  Use the same M both ways.
